''Untrodden'' long, with grass is grown.</poem>

¶
'''untroth†''' (un-trôth′), ''n.'' [A var. of ''untruth'', as ''troth'' is of ''truth''.] '''1.''' Untruth; falsehood.
{{smaller block|<poem>If you find my words to be ''untroth'',
Then let me die to recompense the wrong.</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', Alphonsus, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' An untruth; a falsehood.
{{smaller block|There will be a yard of dissimulation at least, city-measure, and cut upon an ''untroth'' or two.
{{right|''Fletcher and Rowley'', Maid in the Mill, iv. 1.}}}}

'''untrouble†''' (un-trub′l), ''v. t.'' To free from trouble; disabuse. ''Leighton'', Com. on 1 Pet. v.

'''untroubled''' (un-trub′ld), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not troubled; not disturbed by care, sorrow, or business; not agitated; unmoved; unruffled; not confused; free from passion: as, an ''untroubled'' mind.
{{smaller block|Quiet, ''untroubled'' soul, awake!
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., v. 3. 149.}}}}
'''2.''' Not disturbed or raised into waves or ripples: as, an ''untroubled'' sea.—'''3.''' Not foul; not turbid: as, an ''untroubled'' stream.
{{smaller block|Bodies clear and ''untroubled''. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}}

'''untroubledness''' (un-trub′ld-nes), ''n.'' The state of being untroubled; freedom from trouble; unconcern. ''Hammond'', Works, IV. 479.

'''untrowable†''' (un-trō′ạ-bl), ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''trow'' + ''-able''.] Not to be credited; incredi-

'''untruced†''' (un-tröst′), ''a.'' Not interrupted by a truce; truceless.
{{smaller block|<poem>All those four [elements]
Maintain a natural opposition
And ''untruc’d'' war the one against the other.</poem>
{{right|''Middleton'', No Wit Like a Woman’s, iii. 1.}}}}

'''untrue''' (un-trö′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''untrewe'', ''ontrewe'' (= MLG. ''untrūwe'' = G. ''untreu'' = Icel. ''ūtryggr''); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''true''.] '''1.''' Not true to the fact; contrary to the fact; false.
{{smaller block|And he shewed him trewe tidynges and ''vntrewe'', for he made him beleue howe all the countre of Wales wolde gladlye haue hym to be their lorde.
{{right|''Berners'', tr. of Froissart’s Chron., I. 332.}}
By what construction shall any man make those comparisons true, holding that distinction ''untrue?''
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity.}}}}
'''2.''' Not true to one’s duty; not faithful; inconstant; not fulfilling the duties of a husband, wife, vassal, friend, etc.; not to be trusted; false; disloyal.
{{smaller block|Lete vs take hede to saue the peple and the londe fro these ''vn-trewe'' and misbelevynge Sarazins that thus sodenly be entred vpon vs. ''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 174.
<poem>For further I could say this man ’s ''untrue''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lover’s Complaint, l. 169.}}}}
'''3.''' Not true to a standard or rule; varying from

{{smaller block|Thou grand scourge, or second ''untruss'' of the time.

readings.c2s3:
¶
'''untruthfully''' (un-tröth′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In an untruthful manner; falsely; faithlessly.

'''untruthfulness''' (un-tröth′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The character or state of being untruthful; falseness; unveracity.—'''2.''' Inaccuracy; incorrectness: as, the ''untruthfulness'' of a drawing.

'''untuck''' (un-tuk′), ''v. t.'' To unfold or undo; release from being tucked up or fastened.
{{smaller block|For some, ''untuck’d'', descended her sheaved hat.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lover’s Complaint, l. 31.}}}}

'''untuckered''' (un-tuk′ėrd), ''a.'' Wearing no tucker: said of a woman.

'''untufted''' (un-tuf′ted), ''a.'' Without tufts or projecting bunches, as of scales or hairs: specifically noting certain moths.

'''untunable''' (un-tū′na-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not capable of being tuned or brought to the proper pitch.—'''2.''' Not harmonious; discordant; not musical.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then in dumb silence will I bury mine [news],
For they are harsh, ''untuneable'', and bad.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1. 208.}}}}
Also ''untuneable.''

'''untunableness''' (un-tū′nạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being untunable; want of harmony or concord; discord. ''T. Warton.''

'''untunably''' (un-tū′nạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an untunable manner; discordantly. ''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 586.

'''untune''' (un-tūn′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To put out of tune; make incapable of consonance or harmony.
{{smaller block|''Untune'' that string. {{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 3. 109.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
{{smaller block|It requires a long and powerful counter-sympathy in a nation to ''untwine'' the ties of custom which bind a people to the established and the old. {{right|''Sir W. Hamilton.''}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become untwined.
{{smaller block|His silken braids ''untwine'', and slip their knots.
{{right|''Milton'', Divorce, i. 6.}}}}

¶
'''untwist''' (un-twist′), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To separate and open, as threads twisted; turn back from being twisted. ''Swift.''—'''2.''' Figuratively, to disentangle; solve: as, to ''untwist'' a riddle. ''Fletcher'', A Woman Pleased, v. 1.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become separate and loose or straight from having been twisted.

'''untwist''' (un-twist′), ''n.'' [< ''untwist'', ''v.''] A twist in the opposite direction.
{{smaller block|Each coil of the cable in the tank as it comes out receives a twist in the opposite direction, or ''untwist.''
{{right|''Elect. Rev.'' (Eng.), XXIV. 467.}}}}

'''ununderstandable''' (un-un-dėr-stan′dạ-bl), ''a.'' Not to be understood; incomprehensible. ''Piazzi Smyth.'' [Rare.]

'''ununderstood''' (un-un-dėr-stu̇d′), ''a.'' Not understood; not comprehended. ''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., IX. i. 50. [Rare.]

'''ununiform''' (un-ū′ni-fôrm), ''a.'' Not uniform; wanting uniformity. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|An ''ununiform'' piety. {{right|''Decay of Christian Piety.''}}}}

'''ununiformness''' (un-ū′ni-fôrm-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being ununiform; want of uniformity. [Rare.]
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|A variety of parts, or an ''ununiformness.''
{{right|''Clarke,'' Answer to Sixth Letter.}}}}

'''unurged''' (un-ėrjd′), ''a.'' Not urged; not pressed with solicitation; unsolicited; voluntary; of one’s own accord. ''Shak.,'' K. John, v. 2. 10.

'''unusage†''' (un-ū′zāj), ''n.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''usage.''] '''1.''' Unusualness; infrequency.
{{smaller block|Defawte of ''unusage'' and entrecomunynge of marchaundise. {{right|''Chaucer,'' Boëthius, ii. prose 7.}}}}
'''2.''' Want of use. ''Halliwell.''

'''unused''' (un-ūzd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not put to use; not employed; not applied; disused. ''Shak.,'' Sonnets, iv.—'''2.''' That has never been used.—'''3.''' Not accustomed; not habituated: as, hands ''unused'' to labor; hearts ''unused'' to deceit.
{{smaller block|''Unused'' to the melting mood. ''Shak.,'' Othello, v. 2. 349.
<poem>Her gaoler’s torches fill with light
The dreary place, blinding her ''unused'' eyes.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris,'' Earthly Paradise, I. 263.}}}}
'''4.''' Unusual; unwonted.
{{smaller block|<poem>Bitter pain his vexed heart wrought for him,
And filled with ''unused'' tears his hard wise eyes.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris,'' Earthly Paradise, III. 145.}}}}

'''unusedness''' (un-ū′zed-nes), ''n.'' Unwontedness; unusualness. ''Sir P. Sidney,'' Arcadia, vii. [Rare.]

'''unuseful''' (un-ūs′fu̇l), ''a.'' Useless; serving no purpose. ''Jer. Taylor,'' Works (ed. 1835), II. 292.
{{smaller block|<poem>Those hands that gave the casket may the palsy
For ever make ''unuseful,'' even to feed thee!</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher,'' Wife for a Month, i. 2.}}}}

'''unusefully''' (un-ūs′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In a useless manner. ''Jer. Taylor,'' Works (ed. 1835), I. 236.

'''3.''' Not true to a standard or rule; varying from a correct form, pattern, intonation, alinement, or the like; incorrect.
{{smaller block|Henry chastysed the olde ''untrewe'' mesure, and made a yerde of the length of his owne arme.
{{right|''Fabyan'', Chronycle, ccxxvi. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}

In the case of crank-pins wearing ''untrue'', there is nothing for it but filing to caliper.
{{right|''The Engineer'', LXIX. 159.}}}}

'''untrue†''' (un-trö′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''untrewe''; < ''untrue'', ''a.''] Untruly.
{{smaller block|Elles he moot telle his tale ''untrewe''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 735.}}}}

'''untrueness''' (un-trö′nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''untrewenesse''; < ''untrue'' + ''-ness''.] The character of being untrue.

'''untruism''' (un-trö′izm), ''n.'' [< ''untrue'' + ''-ism''.] Something obviously untrue; the opposite of a truism. [A nonce-word.]
{{smaller block|Platitudes, truisms, and ''untruisms''.
{{right|''Trollope'', Barchester Towers, vi.}}}}

'''untruly''' (un-trö′li), ''adv.'' In an untrue manner; not truly; falsely.
{{smaller block|Master More ''untruly'' reporteth of me in his dialogue.
{{right|''Tyndale'', Ans. to Sir T. More, etc. (Parker Soc., 1850), p. 14.}}}}

'''untruss''' (un-trus′), ''v. t.'' To untie or unfasten; loose from a truss, or as from a truss; let out; specifically, to loose, as to let down the breeches by untying the points by which they were held up; undress.
{{smaller block|<poem>Give me my nightcap, so!
Quick, quick, ''untruss'' me.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Elder Brother, iv. 4.}}}}

{{smaller block|Our Muse is in mind for th’ ''untrussing'' a poet.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, v. 1}}
The Clerk of Chatham was ''untrussing'' his points preparatory to seeking his truckle-bed.
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 71}}}}

'''untruss†''' (un-trus′), ''n.'' Same as ''untrusser.''

{{smaller block|Thou grand scourge, or second ''untruss'' of the time.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, ii. 1.}}}}

'''untrussed''' (un-trust′), ''a.'' Not trussed; not tied up; not bundled up. ''Fairfax'', Godfrey of Boulogne, xviii.

<poem>Behold the sacred Pales, where with haire
''Untrust'' she sitts, in shade of yonder hill.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''L. Bryskett'', Pastorall Aeglogue.}}}}

{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, v. 3.}}}}

'''untrust†''' (un-trust′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''untrust'', ''untrist'' (= Icel. ''ūtraust''); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''trust''<sup>1</sup>.] Lack of trust; distrust.

<poem>Ye have noon oother countenance I leeve,
But speke to us of ''untrust'' and repreeve.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 962.}}}}

'''untrust†''', ''a.'' [ME., also ''untriste'' (= Icel. ''utraustr''), faithless: see ''untrust'', ''n.''] Faithless; distrustful.

{{smaller block|Why hastow made Troylus to me ''untriste'' [var. ''untruste'']?
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 839.}}}}

'''untrustful''' (un-trust′fu̇l), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not trustful or trusting.—'''2.''' Not to be trusted; not trustworthy; not trusty. ''Scott.'' [Rare.]

'''untrustiness''' (un-trus′ti-nes), ''n.'' The character of being untrusty; unfaithfulness in the discharge of a trust. ''Sir T. Hayward.''

'''untrustworthiness''' (un-trust′wėr″ᴛ̵ʜi-nes), ''n.'' The character of being untrustworthy.
{{smaller block|Much has been said about ''untrustworthiness'' of historical evidence. ''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., p. 75.}}

'''untrustworthy''' (un-trust′wėr″ᴛ̵ʜi), ''a.'' Not trustworthy, in any sense: as, an ''untrustworthy'' servant; an ''untrustworthy'' boat.
{{smaller block|It wants it [sifting] all the more because it is so closely connected with the early Venetian history, than which no history is more utterly ''untrustworthy''.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 228.}}}}

'''untrusty''' (un-trus′ti), ''a.'' [< ME. ''untrusty'', ''ontrusty'', ''ontristy''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''trusty''.] Not trusty; not worthy of confidence; unfaithful. ''Thomas Lodge'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 14).

'''untruth''' (un-tröth′), ''n.'' [Also ''untroth'', q. v.; < ME. ''ontreuthe'', ''untrouthe'', ''untrowthe'', < AS. ''untreówth'', untruth; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''truth''.] '''1.''' The character of being untrue; contrariety to truth; want of veracity.
{{smaller block|He who is perfect and abhors ''untruth''. ''Sandys.''}}
'''2.''' Treachery; want of fidelity; faithlessness; disloyalty.
{{smaller block|''Untruth'' has made thee subtle in thy trade.
{{right|''Ford'', Lover’s Melancholy, iv. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' A false assertion; a falsehood; a lie.
{{smaller block|Moreover, they have spoken ''untruths''; . . . and, to conclude, they are lying knaves. ''Shak.'', Much Ado, v. 1. 220.}}

'''untruthful''' (un-tröth′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not truthful; wanting in veracity; contrary to the truth. ''Clarke.''

'''untruthfully''' (un-tröth′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In an untruthful manner; falsely; faithlessly.

'''untruthfulness''' (un-tröth′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The character or state of being untruthful; falseness; unveracity.—'''2.''' Inaccuracy; incorrectness: as, the ''untruthfulness'' of a drawing.

'''untuck''' (un-tuk′), ''v. t.'' To unfold or undo; release from being tucked up or fastened.
{{smaller block|For some, ''untuck’d'', descended her sheaved hat.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lover’s Complaint, l. 31.}}}}

'''untuckered''' (un-tuk′ėrd), ''a.'' Wearing no tucker: said of a woman.

'''untufted''' (un-tuf′ted), ''a.'' Without tufts or projecting bunches, as of scales or hairs: specifically noting certain moths.

'''untunable''' (un-tū′na-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not capable of being tuned or brought to the proper pitch.—'''2.''' Not harmonious; discordant; not musical.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then in dumb silence will I bury mine [news],
For they are harsh, ''untuneable'', and bad.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1. 208.}}}}
Also ''untuneable.''

'''untunableness''' (un-tū′nạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being untunable; want of harmony or concord; discord. ''T. Warton.''

'''untunably''' (un-tū′nạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an untunable manner; discordantly. ''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 586.

'''untune''' (un-tūn′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To put out of tune; make incapable of consonance or harmony.
{{smaller block|''Untune'' that string. {{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 3. 109.}}}}
<poem>Naught ''untunes'' that Infant’s voice; no trace
Of fretful temper sullies her pure cheek.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', Sonnets, iii. 16.}}}}

'''2.''' To disorder; confuse.
{{smaller block|''Untuned'' and jarring senses. {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 7. 16.}}}}

'''untuned''' (un-tūnd′), ''a.'' Not tuned; unmusical; unharmonious.
{{smaller block|With boisterous ''untuned'' drums.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., i. 3. 134.}}}}

'''unturf''' (un-tėrf′), ''v. t.'' To remove turf from; deprive of turf. ''Nature'', XLIII. 80.

'''unturn''' (un-tėrn′), ''v. t.'' To turn in the reverse way, as in a manner to open something. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Think you he nought but prison walls did see,
Till, so unwilling, thou ''unturn’dst'' the key?</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', The Day Leigh Hunt Left Prison.}}}}

'''unturned''' (un-tėrnd′), ''a.'' Not turned.—'''To leave no stone unturned.''' {{smaller|See ''stone''.}}

'''untutored''' (un-tū′tọrd), ''a.'' Uninstructed; untaught; rude; raw.
{{smaller block|Some ''untutor’d'' youth. {{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cxxxviii.}}}}

'''untwine''' (un-twīn′), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To untwist; open or separate after having been twisted; untie; disentangle; hence, figuratively, to explain; solve.
{{smaller block|This knot might be ''untwined'' with more facilitie thus.
{{right|''Holinshed'', Sundrie Invasions of Ireland. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}
<poem>On his sad brow nor mirth nor wine
Could e’er one wrinkled knot ''untwine''.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, iii. 22.}}}}

'''2.''' To unwind, as a vine or anything that has been twined around something else: literally or figuratively. {{smaller block|It requires a long and powerful counter-sympathy in a nation to ''untwine'' the ties of custom which bind a people to the established and the old. {{right|''Sir W. Hamilton.''}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become untwined.
{{smaller block|His silken braids ''untwine'', and slip their knots.
{{right|''Milton'', Divorce, i. 6.}}}}

'''untwist''' (un-twist′), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To separate and open, as threads twisted; turn back from being twisted. ''Swift.''—'''2.''' Figuratively, to disentangle; solve: as, to ''untwist'' a riddle. ''Fletcher'', A Woman Pleased, v. 1.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become separate and loose or straight from having been twisted.

'''untwist''' (un-twist′), ''n.'' [< ''untwist'', ''v.''] A twist in the opposite direction.
{{smaller block|Each coil of the cable in the tank as it comes out receives a twist in the opposite direction, or ''untwist.''
{{right|''Elect. Rev.'' (Eng.), XXIV. 467.}}}}

'''ununderstandable''' (un-un-dėr-stan′dạ-bl), ''a.'' Not to be understood; incomprehensible. ''Piazzi Smyth.'' [Rare.]

'''ununderstood''' (un-un-dėr-stu̇d′), ''a.'' Not understood; not comprehended. ''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., IX. i. 50. [Rare.]

'''ununiform''' (un-ū′ni-fôrm), ''a.'' Not uniform; wanting uniformity. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|An ''ununiform'' piety. {{right|''Decay of Christian Piety.''}}}}

'''ununiformness''' (un-ū′ni-fôrm-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being ununiform; want of uniformity. [Rare.] {{smaller block|A variety of parts, or an ''ununiformness.''
{{right|''Clarke,'' Answer to Sixth Letter.}}}}

'''unurged''' (un-ėrjd′), ''a.'' Not urged; not pressed with solicitation; unsolicited; voluntary; of one’s own accord. ''Shak.,'' K. John, v. 2. 10.

'''unusage†''' (un-ū′zāj), ''n.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''usage.''] '''1.''' Unusualness; infrequency.
{{smaller block|Defawte of ''unusage'' and entrecomunynge of marchaundise. {{right|''Chaucer,'' Boëthius, ii. prose 7.}}}}
'''2.''' Want of use. ''Halliwell.''

'''unused''' (un-ūzd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not put to use; not employed; not applied; disused. ''Shak.,'' Sonnets, iv.—'''2.''' That has never been used.—'''3.''' Not accustomed; not habituated: as, hands ''unused'' to labor; hearts ''unused'' to deceit.
{{smaller block|''Unused'' to the melting mood. ''Shak.,'' Othello, v. 2. 349.
<poem>Her gaoler’s torches fill with light
The dreary place, blinding her ''unused'' eyes.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris,'' Earthly Paradise, I. 263.}}}}
'''4.''' Unusual; unwonted.
{{smaller block|<poem>Bitter pain his vexed heart wrought for him,
And filled with ''unused'' tears his hard wise eyes.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris,'' Earthly Paradise, III. 145.}}}}

'''unusedness''' (un-ū′zed-nes), ''n.'' Unwontedness; unusualness. ''Sir P. Sidney,'' Arcadia, vii. [Rare.]

'''unuseful''' (un-ūs′fu̇l), ''a.'' Useless; serving no purpose. ''Jer. Taylor,'' Works (ed. 1835), II. 292.
{{smaller block|<poem>Those hands that gave the casket may the palsy
For ever make ''unuseful,'' even to feed thee!</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher,'' Wife for a Month, i. 2.}}}}

'''unusefully''' (un-ūs′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In a useless manner. ''Jer. Taylor,'' Works (ed. 1835), I. 236.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
